title: AI or Not?
goals: Distinguish an observed result from an explanation of how it was produced
Identify written rules, learned models and human decisions inside one product
Explain what additional evidence is needed when a mechanism is unknown
vocabulary: The process that produces a result
An instruction specified by a person before the system applies it
A system whose adjustable values were fitted using examples
Information that supports or challenges a particular claim
A product that combines more than one kind of process

blocks.text: Question: Does the red display prove that a learned model was used? First separate the claim from the observation. The observation is that the displayed number is red. The claim concerns the process that produced the number. Next find relevant evidence. The engineering note says earlier journeys were used to fit the delay estimator. That note supports a learned-model classification for the estimator. The red colour alone does not.

rows: The estimator uses a learned model
The note describes fitting on past journeys
Only the displayed colour is observed
The driver override is a model prediction
A driver selects the replacement message

blocks.text: A strong answer states its limit: I can identify these three mechanisms from the supplied note, but I cannot infer the model's accuracy from one estimate. Even if the bus arrives exactly 12 minutes late, one success does not establish that the estimator will always work.

guided_practice.title: Complete the photo library explanation
guided_practice.prompt: Use the photo-library case from the lesson. Classify the prediction, album-placement rule and owner move. A bicycle photo is in the wrong album. Name the first two records you would inspect.
guided_practice.answer: Prediction is learned because it was fitted using labelled pictures. Album placement is a written rule; the owner move is human control. Inspect the stored prediction and the placement or move record. A wrong album alone cannot distinguish prediction error from a later action.

independent_case.title: Investigate a new hybrid system
independent_case.task: A school greenhouse estimates tomorrow's temperature using a model fitted on historical weather. A written rule displays CHECK PLANTS above 30 degrees C. A caretaker chooses whether to open a vent. Identify each mechanism and explain why a correct CHECK PLANTS message would not prove an accurate temperature prediction.
independent_case.answer: The forecast is learned-model prediction; the message is a written threshold; vent opening is the caretaker's decision. The message may correctly follow a forecast that is itself inaccurate. Compare the forecast with a predefined temperature observation at the relevant place and time before judging prediction accuracy.
independent_case.source: primary source W4, first curriculum occurrence

misconceptions: Explain that AI also includes symbolic reasoning. In the specific bus case, the simple colour threshold is automation; the full system contains a fitted predictor.
A correct output proves a learned model
Ask whether a calculator, recording or person could produce the same correct output. Require evidence about fitting or reasoning.
Accept unknown when the learner identifies a specific missing fact and a useful way to obtain it.

blocks.text: VISUAL MECHANISM
Input → Process → Output
Follow the information instead of imagining magic inside the machine.

blocks.alt: Visual card for the input stage: a command, signal, photo, sound, or number
Visual card for the process stage: a human choice, fixed instruction, or learned pattern
Visual card for the output stage: movement, calculation, action, or prediction

blocks.text: INPUT  a command, signal, photo, sound, or number
PROCESS  a human choice, fixed instruction, or learned pattern
OUTPUT  movement, calculation, action, or prediction
CORE IDEA  Look for evidence of how the system reasons or learns, not just its label or screen.

UNDER THE HOOD  A system should be classified by its decision mechanism. Human control, fixed automation, and model-based prediction can produce similar visible behavior, so appearance and marketing words are weak evidence.
Draw a fresh example with all three stages:
A closer explanation

blocks.title: The bus display contains three mechanisms
rows: Delay model fitted on earlier journeys
Written rule red when delay is greater than 10
blocks.caption: Read each row from left to right. The first row predicts a number, the second chooses a colour, and the third shows a human override. A correct colour does not establish that the delay prediction is correct.

blocks.text: In the first row, fitting means adjusting a model using examples. Applying the fitted model to a new journey is a different step. The model can produce an incorrect estimate even if it was trained carefully. In the second row, a written threshold compares the estimate with 10. It can follow its instructions perfectly while using a bad estimate. In the third row, a person makes the message decision.

AI is a broader field than learning from examples. It also includes approaches that represent knowledge and reason with rules. Therefore, do not use the shortcut that every rule is non-AI. In this case, a simple colour switch is ordinary automation; identifying that switch does not classify every other part of the bus system.
Connect the picture and the explanation
Point to the input, the deciding step and the result in this week’s visual. Explain the same step in ordinary words. A picture helps when you can say what each part represents.

Comparison picture for Photo sorter: trained model predicts a new label; AI-based

blocks.text: CASE 1 — Remote car  Clue: person sends each steering command. Meaning: human-controlled.
CASE 2 — Motion light  Clue: written if-motion-then-light rule. Meaning: fixed automation.
CASE 3 — Photo sorter  Clue: trained model predicts a new label. Meaning: AI-based.
CASE 4 — Robot vacuum  Clue: description hides the mechanism. Meaning: not enough information.
BOUNDARY  Do not call a system AI because it looks, moves, or talks like a person.
Which two pictures are easiest to confuse? What evidence separates them?
